title: OpenBench Index
subtitle: Aggregated benchmark scores of open-weight LLMs across many benchmark suites.

name.label: Model
name.description: The creator's own name for the model. It links to the model card or release page this row is checked against, and wears the NEW sticker for its first week in the index.

creator.label: Creator
creator.description: The organisation that trained and released the model. It links to that organisation's homepage.

params.label: Params
params.description: Parameter count in the size its creator advertises, with the active count after a dash for a mixture of experts (1T-A32B) and an E prefix for an effective size (E4B).

context.label: Context
context.description: Largest context window the creator advertises, in tokens (128k, 256k, 1m).

columnCards.name: VRAM Requirements
columnCards.description: Single-model inference VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4 precision, estimated by Spheron's per-model GPU recommender. The GPU filter keeps a model when its smallest variant fits the selected budget after the reserve.

openbench_index.name: OpenBench Index
openbench_index.description: Weighted mean of four OpenBench indexes, each an expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000: Coding (0.30), Tooling (0.30), Trust (0.25), Knowledge (0.15). Only models ranked on all four carry a value.

coding_index.name: OpenBench Coding Index
coding_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: Real-SWE 1.1 (1), DeepSWE 1.1 (0.35), FrontierSWE 2.0 (0.9), FrontierCode 2.0 (1), SWE-Marathon 1.1 (0.5), Terminal-Bench 4.0 (0.85), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (0.25), Vibe Code Bench 1.1 (0.5), SWE-bench Pro (0.3), SWE-Bench Pro V2 Hard (0.35), LiveCodeBench (0.25), SciCode (0.35), SWE-bench Multilingual (0.3), SWE Atlas: Codebase Q&A (0.55), SWE Atlas: Refactoring (0.6), SWE Atlas: Test Writing (0.4), ProgramBench: Almost Resolved (0.9), KernelBench Hard (0.4), SWE-bench Verified (0.1), ALE-Bench (0.4), NL2Repo (0.25).

tooling_index.name: OpenBench Tooling Index
tooling_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: AutomationBench-AA (1), Terminal-Bench 4.0 (1), Toolathlon-Verified (0.8), GDPval-AA v2 (0.7), MCP-Atlas (0.7), ITBench-AA (0.6), τ³-Bench Banking (0.5), BFCL v4 (0.45), Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (0.35), Terminal-Bench Hard (0.3), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (0.2), τ²-Bench Telecom (0.15), IFBench (0.15), APEX-Agents (0.5), Vending-Bench 2 (0.35), Claw-Eval (0.3), τ²-Bench Retail (0.2), τ²-Bench Airline (0.2).

knowledge_index.name: OpenBench Knowledge Index
knowledge_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: AA-Omniscience v1 (0.6), AA-Omniscience v1.1 (0.4), Humanity's Last Exam (0.9), CritPt v2 Hard (0.7), CritPt (0.3), MMLU-Pro (0.5), AIME 2025 (0.4), GPQA Diamond (0.3), Humanity's Last Exam Diamond (0.3), FrontierMath Tier 4 (0.6), FrontierMath Tiers 1-3 (0.4), HMMT February 2026 (0.3).

vision_index.name: OpenBench Vision Index
vision_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: MMMU Pro (1), OSWorld-Verified (0.7), MathVista-mini (0.35), ZeroBench (0.35), CharXiv Reasoning (0.35), OSWorld 2.0 2026.06.24 (0.15), OSWorld 2.0 2026.08.08 (0.15), OSWorld 2.0 Vendor (0.15), OSWorld 2.1 (0.2).

trust_index.name: OpenBench Trust Index
trust_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: AA-Omniscience v1 Hallucination Rate (0.6), AA-Omniscience v1.1 Hallucination Rate (0.4), AA-Omniscience v1 Accuracy (0.35), AA-Omniscience v1.1 Accuracy (0.25), AA-LCR (0.45), IFBench (0.3), SimpleQA Verified (0.4), Arena Agent: Tool Hallucination (0.3).

security_index.name: OpenBench Security Index
security_index.description: Weighted Bradley–Terry fit with coverage shrinkage; index = expected win rate against ranked models × 100,000. Weights: ExploitGym (1), CyberBench v1.1 (0.9), CyberBench v1 (0.85), SEC-bench Pro (0.45), SEC-bench Pro 260617 (0.15), CWE-Bench-AA (0.45), DeepsecBench-AA (0.4), CyberGym (0.4).

aa_intelligence_index_5_0.name: AA Intelligence Index v5.0
aa_intelligence_index_5_0.description: Artificial Analysis composite index of overall model capability, v5.0 since 2026-10-27: nine evaluations in four equally weighted categories — Knowledge Work (AA-Briefcase v1.1, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf), Coding (FrontierCode 2.0, Terminal-Bench 4.0), Science (Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, CritPt v2 Hard subset) and General (AA-Omniscience v1.1, HLE-Diamond). GDPval-AA, SciCode, AA-LCR and HLE left the index with this version. Scored on Artificial Analysis' index scale rather than as a percentage; written only while AA's API states version 5.0.
excludes: v4.x index values, on other components and weights

aa_intelligence_index_4_3.name: AA Intelligence Index v4.3
aa_intelligence_index_4_3.description: Artificial Analysis composite index v4.3 (September to October 2026, as read 2026-09-08 to 2026-10-27): AutomationBench-AA replaced τ³-Banking and Terminal-Bench 4.0 replaced 2.1; weights GDPval-AA v2 10%, AA-Briefcase 15%, AutomationBench-AA 5%, Terminal-Bench 4.0 10%, SciCode 10%, AA-LCR 5%, AA-Omniscience 15%, HLE 10%, GDP.pdf 10%, CritPt 10%. Includes the v4.3.1 and v4.3.2 point releases (refreshed judge panels; GDPval-AA v2.1 and AA-Briefcase v1.1 refitted), which moved 56 values on 2026-09-19. Archived: the values this table read while AA served v4.3, restored from llm.json's git history; kept for comparison and for the models never scored on a later version.
excludes: every other index version, on other components and weights

aa_intelligence_index_4_2.name: AA Intelligence Index v4.2
aa_intelligence_index_4_2.description: Artificial Analysis composite index v4.2 (early September 2026, as read 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-07): AA-Briefcase and GDP.pdf added, GPQA Diamond removed, AA-LCR upgraded to v1.1 and SciCode regraded. Archived: the values this table read while AA served v4.2, restored from llm.json's git history; kept for comparison and for the models never scored on a later version.

aa_intelligence_index_4_1.name: AA Intelligence Index v4.1
aa_intelligence_index_4_1.description: Artificial Analysis composite index v4.1 (June to August 2026, as read 2026-06-18 to 2026-09-03): GDPval-AA v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 in place of Terminal-Bench Hard, τ³-Banking in place of τ²-Bench Telecom, IFBench removed; Agents 34%, Coding 24%, Scientific Reasoning 24%, General 18%. Includes v4.1.1 (τ³-Banking dataset and HLE/AA-LCR/Omniscience grader updates). Archived: the values this table read while AA served v4.1, restored from llm.json's git history; kept for comparison and for the models never scored on a later version.

aa_intelligence_index_4_0.name: AA Intelligence Index v4.0
aa_intelligence_index_4_0.description: Artificial Analysis composite index v4.0 (January to June 2026, as read until 2026-06-17): GDPval-AA, AA-Omniscience and CritPt added, MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025 removed; four categories at 25% each. aa_coding_index_4_1.name: AA Coding Index v4.1
aa_coding_index_4_1.description: Artificial Analysis' coding sub-index as it stood under Intelligence Index v4.1 (as read 2026-06-25 until the column was dropped at the end of August): the average of Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SciCode. AA no longer publishes it as a field; archived from llm.json's git history. Not aggregated: its inputs are columns of their own.
excludes: the Coding Agent Index, which runs models inside vendors' agents

aa_coding_index_4_0.name: AA Coding Index v4.0
aa_coding_index_4_0.description: Artificial Analysis' coding sub-index as it stood under Intelligence Index v4.0 (as read until 2026-06-24): the average of Terminal-Bench Hard and SciCode. AA no longer publishes it as a field; archived from llm.json's git history. Not aggregated: its inputs are columns of their own.
excludes: the Coding Agent Index, which runs models inside vendors' agents

aa_cyber_index.name: AA Cyber Index
aa_cyber_index.description: Artificial Analysis' composite of three defensive cybersecurity evaluations it runs itself on every model: CWE-Bench-AA (audit a codebase, find a vulnerability in a described area and patch it), DeepsecBench-AA (find vulnerabilities in real application code, scored by F2) and CyberGym-E2E-AA (find, reproduce and patch real memory-safety bugs in C/C++ projects). A refusal counts as a failure, so the index measures what a model will do as well as what it can: a model that refuses the tasks scores far below its capability (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Sol and both Qwen3.8 models refuse 98-100% of CyberGym-E2E). Scored 0 to 100 on Artificial Analysis' index scale.
excludes: unmitigated variants AA lists beside a model's standard release

aa_engineering_index.name: AA Engineering Index
aa_engineering_index.description: Artificial Analysis' Engineering domain index: AA's composite score for engineering work, published per model beside the Intelligence Index (API field artificial_analysis_engineering_index) on its index scale. AA documents no version for it; a change of formula would show as a coordinated shift in the column, which the refresh reports.

aa_strategy_ops_index.name: AA Strategy & Ops Index
aa_strategy_ops_index.description: Artificial Analysis' Strategy & Ops domain index: AA's composite score for strategy & ops work, published per model beside the Intelligence Index (API field artificial_analysis_strategy_and_ops_index) on its index scale. AA documents no version for it; a change of formula would show as a coordinated shift in the column, which the refresh reports.

aa_healthcare_index.name: AA Healthcare & Medical Index
aa_healthcare_index.description: Artificial Analysis' Healthcare & Medical domain index: AA's composite score for healthcare & medical work, published per model beside the Intelligence Index (API field artificial_analysis_healthcare_and_medical_index) on its index scale. Its components include MLCR-AA, AA's medical long-context reasoning evaluation. AA documents no version for it; a change of formula would show as a coordinated shift in the column, which the refresh reports.

aa_legal_index.name: AA Legal Index

AA documents no version for it; a change of formula would show as a coordinated shift in the column, which the refresh reports.

AA documents no version for it; a change of formula would show as a coordinated shift in the column, which the refresh reports.

real_swe_1_1.name: Real-SWE 1.1
real_swe_1_1.description: Coding agents on private, real-world enterprise codebases: tasks lifted from production repositories licensed from real companies, so neither the code, the ticket nor the reference solution exists on the public internet. Release 1.1 (October 2026) expands the benchmark to 25 tasks across TypeScript, Go, Python, Ruby and Java codebases. Tasks are graded by verifiers built from each repository's own test suite and injected at grading time. Scores are the resolution rate — pass@1 averaged over eight independent runs per task — for a model run in its native agent harness, so a row measures a model-and-harness pair.

real_swe_1_0.name: Real-SWE 1.0
real_swe_1_0.description: The first release of Real-SWE (September 2026): 10 tasks from private production codebases licensed from real companies, graded by verifiers built from each repository's own test suite; pass@1 averaged over eight runs per task, each model in its native harness. Replaced by 1.1 on the same page on 2026-10-15 without its board being kept, so this column holds the values read before the switch and receives no new ones.

deepswe_1_1.name: DeepSWE 1.1
deepswe_1_1.description: Benchmark measuring frontier coding agents on original, long-horizon and hand-written software engineering tasks on active open-source repositories; Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go and Rust. Revision 1.1 is the current leaderboard, re-run in September 2026; its numbers are not comparable with 1.0's, which moved some models by more than 50 points.
excludes: DeepSWE 1.0, which moved some models by more than 50 points

deepswe_1_0.name: DeepSWE 1.0
deepswe_1_0.description: Benchmark measuring frontier coding agents on original, long-horizon and hand-written software engineering tasks on active open-source repositories; Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go and Rust. Revision 1.0 is the superseded June 2026 run, still published beside the current one and the only revision that scored the models retired before the re-run. Kept as a separate column because its scores are not comparable with 1.1's, and left out of the coding index for the same reason.

frontiercode_2_0.name: FrontierCode 2.0
frontiercode_2_0.description: Cognition's benchmark of hard, hand-crafted software engineering tasks graded on whether a maintainer would merge the change. Revision 2.0 (2026-10-27) rebuilds the suite to evaluate user experience: 132 tasks spanning more repositories and categories, including security patches and performance optimizations, with higher mergeability standards and more emphasis on thoroughness. The score is a weighted aggregate of rubric items, zero for a solution that fails a blocking criterion. Cognition's board and Artificial Analysis' own implementation, which outranks it where both report; not comparable with 1.x.

frontiercode_extended_1_1.name: FrontierCode 1.1 Extended
frontiercode_extended_1_1.description: Cognition's benchmark of exceptionally hard, hand-crafted software engineering tasks at the frontier of model capability, graded on whether the change would be merged: each task is scored against reviewer-defined criteria covering correctness, tests, scope, style and repository conventions, some of them blockers that cap the score on their own. Extended is the full 150-task set; the Main column is the 100 hardest of those same tasks, scored from the same runs, so Extended reads about thirteen points higher and Cognition publishes the two as separate leaderboards that are not to be mixed. Revision 1.1 is the current re-run: it allows fair internet use such as documentation and API references, and zeroes any run its scanner catches opening a solution-bearing page. 1.0's Extended board is published too but is not kept as a column.
excludes: the Main board, the 100 hardest of the same tasks

frontiercode_1_1.name: FrontierCode 1.1
frontiercode_1_1.description: Cognition's benchmark of exceptionally hard, hand-crafted software engineering tasks at the frontier of model capability; contamination-resistant and unsaturated -- this board's leader sits at 53.5%. Revision 1.1 re-ran a subset of 1.0's models and was superseded by 2.0 on 2026-10-27; its scores are comparable with neither. This is the Main board, the 100 hardest of the benchmark's 150 tasks; Artificial Analysis' own run of it outranks Cognition's number where both report. The coding index aggregates the Extended board instead: the two are one set of runs scored twice and rank the same field almost identically, so counting both would spend two slots on one measurement, and Extended is the larger sample.
excludes: the Extended board, which reads about 13 points higher off the same runs

frontiercode_1_0.name: FrontierCode 1.0
frontiercode_1_0.description: Cognition's benchmark of exceptionally hard, hand-crafted software engineering tasks at the frontier of model capability; contamination-resistant and unsaturated -- this board's leader scored 46.8%. Revision 1.0 is the superseded run, still published beside the current one and the only revision that scored the models retired before the re-run. Kept as a separate column because its scores are not comparable with 1.1's, and left out of the coding index for the same reason.

frontierswe_2_0.name: FrontierSWE 2.0
frontierswe_2_0.description: Benchmarking software engineering skill at the edge of human ability; 34 hand-crafted tasks run five times each under a 20-hour budget, scored as the mean@5 task score (%). Revision 2.0 is the current board; its scores are not comparable with 1.0's, which ranked a different task set by a pairwise win rate.

frontierswe_1_0.name: FrontierSWE 1.0
frontierswe_1_0.description: Benchmarking software engineering skill at the edge of human ability. Revision 1.0 is the first release, preserved as published at /v1 and the only revision that scored the models retired before the re-run. It ranked 17 tasks by average per-task rank and by dominance -- the win rate against a random opponent on a random task -- and this column stores that dominance as a percentage, the only quantity the board publishes on a higher-is-better 0-100 scale. Kept as a separate column because a win rate is not the 2.0 board's mean@5 task score, and left out of the coding index for the same reason.

programbench_almost.name: ProgramBench: Almost Resolved
programbench_almost.description: Rebuilding a program from scratch: the agent is handed a reference executable and its documentation and nothing else, and has to implement a codebase whose behaviour matches, graded by hidden behavioural tests against the binary it produces. The 200 tasks run from compact CLI tools up to FFmpeg, SQLite and the PHP interpreter, and published runs use mini-SWE-agent with the internet switched off. This column stores Almost Resolved — at least 95% of a task's behavioural tests passing — because the board's primary metric, Resolved, requires every test to pass and is close to the floor today.
excludes: Resolved, the board's primary metric, which requires every test to pass

kernelbench_hard.name: KernelBench Hard
kernelbench_hard.description: Agentic GPU kernel engineering on kernelbench.com: a coding agent gets a reference PyTorch module and an unlimited budget to replace it with a faster kernel on real hardware, and every published cell is audited for reward hacking. This column holds the board's Hard deck -- six problems (FP8 GEMM, KDA on CUTLASS, paged attention, top-k bitonic sort, a Sonic MoE SwiGLU, W4A16 GEMM) on the RTX PRO 6000 the site calls canonical -- as the mean fraction of the GPU's roofline the submitted kernels reach, a failed, flagged or missing problem counting as zero. It is an absolute number, the one labs report as KernelBench Hard (operator TFLOPs over theoretical peak, averaged over the questions), not the site's share of the best model. The site borrows Stanford's KernelBench name and problem style but is not affiliated with it.

nl2repo.name: NL2Repo
nl2repo.description: NL2Repo-Bench: the agent is given a natural-language specification of a whole Python library and an empty workspace, and must build the repository from scratch; the result is scored by the share of the original project's test suite it passes. The only column that measures building a codebase rather than changing one. Lab self-reports, in harnesses that vary from a minimal in-house loop to Claude Code.

vibe_code_bench_1_1.name: Vibe Code Bench 1.1
vibe_code_bench_1_1.description: Vals AI's greenfield application benchmark: the model is handed a natural-language specification for a web application and has to build the running product from scratch in an agent harness. Scoring is behavioural — an autonomous browser agent drives the deployed application against the specification's workflows, so a build that does not run scores nothing. The suite is 100 specifications, 50 public and 50 held out, and it is the one coding column here that measures construction rather than maintenance. Revision 1.1 replaced 1.0 at the same URL, so 1.0's numbers are not comparable and are not kept as a column.
excludes: Vibe Code Bench 1.0, which was replaced at the same URL

ale_bench.name: ALE-Bench
ale_bench.description: Sakana AI and AtCoder's benchmark of long-horizon algorithm engineering: score-based optimisation problems from the AtCoder Heuristic Contests, where there is no single correct answer and a solution is iterated on to push its score up. Each submission is scored against the contest's human field and turned into an AtCoder performance rating, so the column does not saturate the way a pass/fail suite does. Read from Epoch AI's copy of the board.
excludes: ALE-Bench Lite, a smaller problem set

swe_bench_pro_hard_2_0.name: SWE-Bench Pro V2 Hard
swe_bench_pro_hard_2_0.description: The Hard subset of SWE-Bench Pro V2: the 51 of its 642 tasks that proved most challenging across models, run under the same network-locked protocol and published as its own table on Scale's V2 board. It still separates the leaders where the Full set has saturated (the top runs there are within a point of each other). Metric is Pass@1 over the subset.

swe_bench_pro_2_0.name: SWE-Bench Pro V2
swe_bench_pro_2_0.description: Scale AI's refreshed public split of SWE-Bench Pro, co-developed with Reflection and released in September 2026: 642 tasks across the same 11 repositories, after 89 of v1's 731 public instances were dropped as invalid, with every instruction, verifier and image rebuilt and 69 instructions that contradicted their tests corrected. The protocol is network-locked -- the agent's sandbox reaches the model endpoint and nothing else -- and each diff is re-graded on a clean image. Scores sit on another scale from v1's: current models run 87-99 here against at most about 62 on Scale's v1 board, so the two are separate columns. Metric is Pass@1 over the full set.
excludes: the original SWE-bench Pro and its splits

swe_bench_pro.name: SWE-bench Pro
swe_bench_pro.description: Successor to SWE-bench Verified for realistic software engineering tasks; spans Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Go, and is designed to be more contamination-resistant and industry-relevant.
excludes: SWE-Bench Pro V2, a refreshed split on another scale

swe_marathon_1_1.name: SWE-Marathon 1.1
swe_marathon_1_1.description: Ultra-long-horizon agentic software engineering: 20 multi-hour tasks (library reproductions, full-stack product clones, ML engineering), each with an executable environment, a human-written reference solution and a multi-layer verification suite; logged attempts average 27.2M tokens per task. Revision 1.1 is the current board: all 20 tasks updated, with tighter verification and closed-internet execution. The site reuses no 1.0 score for the updated tasks, so the two are not comparable.

swe_marathon_1_0.name: SWE-Marathon 1.0
swe_marathon_1_0.description: Ultra-long-horizon agentic software engineering: 20 multi-hour tasks (library reproductions, full-stack product clones, ML engineering), each with an executable environment, a human-written reference solution and a multi-layer verification suite; logged attempts average 27.2M tokens per task. Revision 1.0 is the archived board the site keeps beside the current one. Kept as a separate column because its scores are not comparable with 1.1's, and left out of the coding index for the same reason.

swe_atlas_rf.name: SWE Atlas: Refactoring
swe_atlas_rf.description: Refactoring track of Scale AI's SWE Atlas suite: restructure production code to improve readability and maintainability while preserving behavior; 70 tasks graded by programmatic test validation plus rubric assessment. Metric is Task Resolve Rate (% of tasks passing all rubric items).
excludes: the Test Writing and Codebase Q&A tracks

swe_atlas_tw.name: SWE Atlas: Test Writing
swe_atlas_tw.description: Test Writing track of Scale AI's SWE Atlas suite: write meaningful tests that exercise real functionality and raise coverage; 90 tasks graded by manifest check, mutation testing and rubric assessment. Metric is Task Resolve Rate (% of tasks passing all rubric items).
excludes: the Refactoring and Codebase Q&A tracks

swe_atlas_qna.name: SWE Atlas: Codebase Q&A
swe_atlas_qna.description: Codebase Q&A track of Scale AI's SWE Atlas suite: deep code-comprehension tasks such as tracing execution paths, multi-file reasoning and answering technical questions, with no code changes required; 124 tasks across 11 open-source repos in Go, Python, C and TypeScript. Metric is Task Resolve Rate (% of tasks passing all rubric items).
excludes: the Refactoring and Test Writing tracks

swe_bench_verified.name: SWE-bench Verified
swe_bench_verified.description: Human-validated subset of SWE-bench for fixing real GitHub issues; solutions are judged by running unit tests.

swe_bench_multimodal.name: SWE-bench Multimodal
swe_bench_multimodal.description: Multimodal extension of SWE-bench: 517 issues from JavaScript and TypeScript repositories whose reports carry visual context — screenshots, design mockups, diagrams — so the fix depends on reading the images, not just the text. Solutions are judged by running unit tests.

swe_bench_multilingual.name: SWE-bench Multilingual
swe_bench_multilingual.description: Multilingual extension of SWE-bench: 300 issue/pull-request pairs from 42 repositories in nine languages other than Python (C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, Rust), collected and graded by the same protocol as SWE-bench -- fail-to-pass tests prove the issue is fixed, pass-to-pass tests prove nothing else broke. Built because agent scaffolds had overfitted to Python tooling. The official leaderboard runs a standardized mini-SWE-agent; a lab self-report uses whatever harness the lab chose.

livecodebench.name: LiveCodeBench
livecodebench.description: Contamination-resistant coding benchmark that continuously collects new problems; evaluates code generation, self-repair, code execution, and test output prediction.
excludes: the v3 and v5 releases, which are smaller problem sets
date windows that name no release
card labels that report it as a 0-1 fraction

scicode.name: SciCode
scicode.description: Scientific coding benchmark evaluating code generation and problem solving in scientific domains.

terminal_bench_4_0.name: Terminal-Bench 4.0
terminal_bench_4_0.description: Current Terminal-Bench release: 66 tasks in sandboxed terminal environments, each with its own verifier. 4.0 recalibrated every task's time, CPU and memory budget to an 8-hour flat agent timeout, removed 8 tasks (2 saturated, 2 refused, 2 with public solutions, 2 unresolved) and fixed 19 others, so it has measurably fewer agent timeouts and errors than 3.0. Scored as the share of tasks resolved, reported with a 95% interval over repeated trials.
excludes: runs named for a harness (Claude Code, Terminus-2)

terminal_bench_3_0.name: Terminal-Bench 3.0
terminal_bench_3_0.description: The Terminal-Bench release before 4.0: 74 tasks in sandboxed terminal environments, each with its own verifier, scored as the share of tasks resolved. Superseded by 4.0, which removed 8 of its tasks and recalibrated every task's time and resource budget, so the two are separate columns. Rows are a model under the agent its submitter ran — Codex, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent — taking each model's best.

terminal_bench_2_1.name: Terminal-Bench 2.1
terminal_bench_2_1.description: Terminal-Bench 2.1 is a collection of tasks and an evaluation harness to help agent makers quantify their agents' terminal mastery.
excludes: “best harness” rows, a maximum over configurations

terminal_bench_2_0.name: Terminal-Bench 2.0
terminal_bench_2_0.description: Terminal-Bench 2.0 is a collection of tasks and an evaluation harness to help agent makers quantify their agents' terminal mastery.

terminal_bench_hard.name: Terminal-Bench Hard
terminal_bench_hard.description: Hard subset of Terminal-Bench tasks; benchmark of real terminal tasks in sandboxed environments with test scripts.

terminal_bench_science_0_1.name: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1
terminal_bench_science_0_1.description: Research workflows in a terminal: 70 tasks authored and reviewed by practising scientists across the life, physical, earth, mathematical and engineering sciences, each with its own verifier. Scored as the share of tasks resolved, pass@1 averaged over three trials per task. A sibling of Terminal-Bench on the same Harbor framework, not a revision of it. Artificial Analysis runs every model under mini-SWE-agent; tbench.ai's own board and Vals AI's run each model under the agent its submitter chose (Codex, Claude Code, …), so the Artificial Analysis run lands wherever it reports.

toolathlon.name: Toolathlon-Verified
toolathlon.description: The Tool Decathlon: long-horizon agentic tool use across 32 real MCP servers plus 7 local toolkits, with 108 tasks averaging around 20 interaction steps. Grading is execution-based on the final state of the applications. Scores are the Toolathlon-Verified series, not comparable with earlier Toolathlon numbers. Metric is Pass@1.
excludes: pre-Verified Toolathlon numbers, a different score series

mcp_atlas.name: MCP-Atlas
mcp_atlas.description: Scale AI's MCP tool-use benchmark: 1,000 human-authored tasks over 40+ real MCP servers exposing 300+ tools, each needing several dependent tool calls picked out from distractors, graded by an LLM judge against the ground-truth answer. The leaderboard runs the representative 500-task public subset under the April 2026 configuration, which replaced the original 20-turn cap with a budget of 100 tool calls per task. Metric is pass rate.
excludes: MCPMark and MCP Mark Verified, a different benchmark

claw_eval.name: Claw-Eval
claw_eval.description: A benchmark of real-world agent tasks run in a claw-style agent harness, each over three trials and scored for completion, safety and robustness. The column holds the score on the 161-task General split — core service-orchestration tasks across 24 categories — as the official leaderboard prints it, carried into the models' Hugging Face eval results.
excludes: pass@3 and pass^3 figures quoted on their own

automation_bench_aa.name: AutomationBench-AA
automation_bench_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' run of Zapier's AutomationBench on a held-out set: 657 end-to-end business workflows across finance, HR, marketing, operations, sales and support, in a simulated company whose apps (CRM, Slack, Google Workspace and dozens more) are reachable only through REST endpoints the agent must discover by search. The agent must chain interdependent API calls, follow layered business-policy documents and ignore planted distractions. Scored with partial credit per completed objective; any guardrail violation zeroes the task. It replaced τ³-Bench Banking in AA's Intelligence Index v4.3 (2026-09-07).
excludes: Zapier's own AutomationBench leaderboard and lab-reported AutomationBench pass rates (pass/fail, a different scale)

vending_bench_2.name: Vending-Bench 2
vending_bench_2.description: Andon Labs' long-horizon agent benchmark: the model runs a simulated vending-machine business for a full simulated year — ordering stock from suppliers by email, negotiating prices, setting prices and handling refunds — starting from a $500 balance. The score is the money balance the year ends on, averaged over runs, so it measures whether an agent stays coherent over thousands of steps rather than whether it can finish one task. Read from Epoch AI's copy of the board.

tau3_bench_banking.name: τ³-Bench Banking
tau3_bench_banking.description: Banking domain of τ³-Bench, as run by Artificial Analysis. τ³ adds a knowledge-retrieval layer to the dual-control τ² setup: action tools are hidden in knowledge-base documents, so the agent must search for them and unlock them with meta-tools before calling. Metric is task success rate.

tau2_bench_telecom.name: τ²-Bench Telecom
tau2_bench_telecom.description: Dual-control conversational agent benchmark where both agent and user use tools in a shared environment; includes a compositional task generator; Telecom domain.
excludes: τ³-Bench, which adds a retrieval layer

tau2_bench_retail.name: τ²-Bench Retail
tau2_bench_retail.description: Retail domain of Sierra's τ²-Bench: the agent serves a simulated customer over several turns — looking up orders, exchanging and returning items — through the domain's tools, under a written policy it must follow. A task passes when the database ends in the expected state. Unlike Telecom, the domain still separates the field. Lab self-reports, under each lab's own prompts and trial counts.

tau2_bench_airline.name: τ²-Bench Airline
tau2_bench_airline.description: Airline domain of Sierra's τ²-Bench: 50 customer-service tasks — booking changes, cancellations, baggage and compensation — handled through the domain's tools under a written policy, with a simulated customer on the other side. A task passes when the reservation database ends in the expected state. Lab self-reports, under each lab's own prompts and trial counts.

bfcl_v4.name: BFCL v4
bfcl_v4.description: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard V4, the Gorilla team's function-calling benchmark grown from single tool calls into holistic agentic evaluation: AST-checked simple, multiple and parallel calls over both curated and live user-contributed functions, multi-turn sessions that withhold a function or a parameter, V4's web-search and memory tracks, relevance and irrelevance detection, and format sensitivity. The reported number is the leaderboard's Overall Accuracy, the unweighted average of every sub-category, taking the better of a model's native function-calling and prompted runs. V4 scores are a series of their own and are not comparable with V1-V3 numbers.
excludes: BFCL v1-v3, a score series of their own

ifbench.name: IFBench
ifbench.description: Ai2's test of whether instruction following generalizes: 58 new, diverse output constraints held out from the small set of verifiable constraints models have overfit to, each checked by a verification function rather than a judge, so a response either satisfies the constraint or does not. Run independently by Artificial Analysis. Metric is the share of constraints satisfied.
excludes: IFEval, the set these constraints were held out from
labels naming one scoring axis only (“prompt”, “loose”)

itbench_aa.name: ITBench-AA
itbench_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' independent implementation of IBM's ITBench, SRE track: 59 Kubernetes incident scenarios (40 from IBM's public release, 19 shared privately by the ITBench team) in which the agent, given shell access to an offline snapshot of alerts, events, traces, metrics and application topology, must identify the entities that caused the failure. Metric is average precision at full recall: a task scores TP/(TP+FP) when no contributing factor is missed, 0 otherwise.

gdpval_aa.name: GDPval-AA v2
gdpval_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' v2.1 evaluation framework over OpenAI's GDPval dataset: 220 real work deliverables — documents, slides, spreadsheets, diagrams — for 44 occupations across 9 industries, authored with experienced professionals. The model works in AA's Stirrup agentic harness with shell access to a sandbox filesystem and web browsing, so a deliverable is the product of a tool trajectory rather than a single response. Scored by blind pairwise LLM-judge comparisons aggregated into an Elo in which 1000 is human expert performance.

apex_agents.name: APEX-Agents
apex_agents.description: Mercor's AI Productivity Index for agents: long-horizon tasks written by investment bankers, management consultants and corporate lawyers, each carried out inside a simulated work environment of files and applications and graded against an expert rubric. The column is pass@1, the share of tasks whose deliverable passes. Read from Epoch AI's copy of Mercor's board.
excludes: the rubric mean score, a different metric

agents_last_exam_1_1.name: Agents' Last Exam v1.1
agents_last_exam_1_1.description: Berkeley RDI's benchmark of long-horizon, economically valuable computer work, authored with 300+ industry experts across 55 professional sub-industries. Each task is graded by a task-specific deterministic grader against a hidden reference. Release v1.1: 122 tasks, the board the leaderboard opens on. Stored value is the Pass Rate — the share of tasks fully passed — taking each model's best harness and variant; the partial-credit Score is a separate scale and is not stored here.

agents_last_exam_1_0.name: Agents' Last Exam v1.0
agents_last_exam_1_0.description: Berkeley RDI's benchmark of long-horizon, economically valuable computer work, authored with 300+ industry experts across 55 professional sub-industries. Each task is graded by a task-specific deterministic grader against a hidden reference. Stored value is the Overall Pass Rate over v1.0's public task set (152 tasks) — the share of tasks fully passed — which is the view the leaderboard opens on; the partial-credit Score and the Near-term, Full-Spectrum, Last-Exam and ALE-CLI tiers are separate scales and are not stored here. Archived: v1.0 is the legacy board since v1.1 (122 tasks) became the one the site opens on.
excludes: the Near-term, Full-Spectrum, Last-Exam and ALE-CLI tiers

aa_briefcase.name: AA-Briefcase
aa_briefcase.description: Artificial Analysis' agentic knowledge-work benchmark: four multi-week project scenarios — data science, product management, banking operations and heavy-industry strategy — totalling 91 tasks over thousands of input files, each producing a professional deliverable (spreadsheets, presentations, documents). Scored as a composite Elo aggregating binary rubric checks with pairwise LLM-judged analytical quality and presentation; GPT-5.5 (medium) anchors 1000.

browsecomp.name: BrowseComp
browsecomp.description: Browsing benchmark with 1,266 challenging short-answer questions designed to be hard to find but easy to verify.
excludes: runs with a bolted-on context manager
BrowseComp+, Top100 and BrowseComp-ZH, different question sets

arena_text.name: Arena Text
arena_text.description: Arena's (formerly LMArena) Text leaderboard: people put their own prompts to two anonymous models, vote for the better answer, and the votes are fitted into a Bradley-Terry rating. The style-controlled board, the one arena.ai shows by default, which regresses out the pull of longer and more heavily formatted answers. The only column in the table set by human preference rather than an automatic checker or a model judge.
excludes: the raw board without style control

arena_text_non_english.name: Arena Text (non-English)
arena_text_non_english.description: The non-English category of Arena's style-controlled Text leaderboard: the same pairwise votes, restricted to prompts written in a language other than English. Human preference on multilingual use, where most open models' cards report nothing.
excludes: single-language categories such as German or Chinese

arena_webdev.name: Arena Code (WebDev)
arena_webdev.description: Arena's Code Arena (formerly WebDev Arena): two anonymous models each build a working web app from the user's request, the user tries both and votes, and the votes are fitted into a Bradley-Terry rating. Human preference on the finished, running result rather than on the code.
excludes: the Text arena's coding category, which votes on answers rather than built apps

arena_agent.name: Arena Agent
arena_agent.description: Agent Arena's aggregate: the model runs real users' agent sessions, and signals from those sessions — whether the task got done, how the user reacted, how reliably shell commands ran, whether tools were hallucinated — are combined into an inverse-propensity-weighted effect relative to the field's average. Stored ×100, so 0 is an average agent and the sign says which side of it a model falls.
excludes: the per-signal scores on their own

arena_agent_tool_hallucination.name: Arena Agent: Tool Hallucination
arena_agent_tool_hallucination.description: Agent Arena's tool-hallucination signal on its own: how often, in real users' agent sessions, the model calls a tool that does not exist or with arguments the tool does not take, as an inverse-propensity-weighted effect relative to the field's average. Stored ×100 and oriented like the aggregate, so higher means fewer hallucinated tool calls; 0 is the field average.

cwe_bench_aa.name: CWE-Bench-AA
cwe_bench_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' implementation of Collinear AI's CWE-bench: a coding agent audits a real open-source codebase, finds a vulnerability in a described area of concern and patches it without breaking legitimate behaviour. A refusal counts as a failed task; the share refused is shown beside each score. One of the three components of the AA Cyber Index.
excludes: Collinear's own CWE-bench leaderboard and lab-reported CWE-bench runs, on other harnesses
unmitigated variants AA lists beside a model's standard release

deepsec_bench_aa.name: DeepsecBench-AA
deepsec_bench_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' implementation of Vercel's DeepsecBench: an agent reviews real open-source application code and reports the vulnerabilities it finds, scored by F2, which weights recall above precision. A refusal counts as a failed task; the share refused is shown beside each score. One of the three components of the AA Cyber Index.
excludes: unmitigated variants AA lists beside a model's standard release

cybergym_e2e_aa.name: CyberGym-E2E-AA
cybergym_e2e_aa.description: Artificial Analysis' implementation of Berkeley RDI's CyberGym-E2E: an agent finds a real memory-safety vulnerability in a C/C++ open-source project, reproduces it with a proof-of-concept input and patches it without breaking the project's tests. End to end, unlike the CyberGym column's Level 1, which hands the agent the vulnerability's description and asks only for a crashing input. A refusal counts as a failed task; the share refused is shown beside each score, and on this component it decides most frontier closed models' results. One of the three components of the AA Cyber Index.
excludes: CyberGym Level 1 runs, which are the cybergym column
unmitigated variants AA lists beside a model's standard release

cybergym.name: CyberGym
cybergym.description: Real-world vulnerability reproduction: 1,507 historical OSS-Fuzz vulnerabilities across 188 C/C++ projects. At Level 1, the one the board ranks, the agent gets a description of the vulnerability and the unpatched codebase and must write a proof-of-concept input that makes the program crash. Graded by running the PoC under a sanitizer, not by a judge. The score depends heavily on the harness: security vendors' multi-stage agents built on the same model score far higher than the model in a plain coding agent, so the column keeps only rows the board marks as measuring a model. Almost every value is the model's own vendor reporting it, in the vendor's own agent or Claude Code.
excludes: agent-focused rows, a security vendor's pipeline around the model
pass@10 runs, which the board's score_10 field mixes in on its 2025 rows
Levels 0, 2 and 3, which give the agent less or more to go on

exploitgym.name: ExploitGym
exploitgym.description: Turning a known vulnerability into a working attack: 869 tasks (502 userspace C/C++, 181 V8, 186 Linux kernel). The agent starts from a crashing proof-of-vulnerability input and must build an exploit that captures a secret flag, with privilege escalation required on the kernel tasks; mitigations are off for the headline count. A flag counts only when a judge confirms the exploit used the intended vulnerability. Scored as the share of the 869 tasks solved on target, single run, at the 6-hour budget vendors report (the maintainers' own runs use 2 hours). Far from saturated, but floor-compressed: most models below the frontier solve almost none.
excludes: the 2-hour budget, which solves 10-35% fewer tasks for the same model
raw task counts such as "105 / 130" on model cards, which are solved tasks rather than percentages
rows run on a selected subset of tasks

exploitbench.name: ExploitBench
exploitbench.description: A capability ladder toward a working V8 exploit: 41 real V8 N-day bugs reported in 2024 or later, each scored by which of five exploitation tiers the agent reaches, from triggering the bug up to arbitrary code execution. The score is the mean coverage of the ladder across tasks and seeds, at a 300-turn budget. Small (41 tasks, one target), and the top of the field is already near the ceiling on vendor self-reports.
excludes: AutoNudge runs, where the harness prompts the agent to keep going
the similarly named ExploitGym, a different benchmark
the "ExploitBench HARD" split some cards claim, which the benchmark does not have

sec_bench_pro_260617.name: SEC-bench Pro 260617
sec_bench_pro_260617.description: The June 2026 snapshot of SEC-bench Pro (260617): the same proof-of-concept task as 260505 — write a PoC for a real vulnerability from a vague report, no crash trace, patch or reference PoC, judged on the vulnerable and the fixed build — over 344 tasks, adding 137 Linux kernel tasks to V8 and SpiderMonkey. It is the snapshot the site root shows. Scores run higher than on 260505 for the same model (GPT-5.5: 58.4 against 46.4), so the two are separate columns. Timeouts count as failures.
excludes: the completed-only rate, which leaves timeouts out

sec_bench_pro.name: SEC-bench Pro
sec_bench_pro.description: Writing a proof of concept for a real vulnerability in a very large codebase, from a vague report: the agent gets the source tree, an instrumented binary and broad vulnerability categories, and no crash trace, patch or reference PoC. A PoC counts only if it triggers on the vulnerable build, not on the fixed one, and an audited LLM judge confirms it is legitimate. This column is the May 2026 snapshot (260505): 183 tasks in V8 and SpiderMonkey, the one vendors report and the maintainers' board still publishes. Timeouts count as failures.
excludes: the 260617 snapshot, 344 tasks with the Linux kernel added
the completed-only rate, which leaves timeouts out
the original SEC-bench's PoC-generation and patching boards

cyberbench_1_1.name: CyberBench v1.1
cyberbench_1_1.description: Vals AI's own security benchmark: an agent crafts a proof-of-concept input that triggers a real OSS-Fuzz vulnerability, then writes a source patch that fixes it, on a private task set Vals runs every model through on its own harness. The column is the board's headline, which pools the PoC and patch tasks; patching is near its ceiling for every model measured (82-88%), so the spread comes from the PoC half. The one security column no lab self-reports.
excludes: the PoC-only and patch-only task scores
CyberGym, an unrelated benchmark on similar OSS-Fuzz material

cyberbench_1_0.name: CyberBench v1
cyberbench_1_0.description: The first revision of Vals AI's own security benchmark, superseded by v1.1 and archived: an agent crafts a proof-of-concept input that triggers a real OSS-Fuzz vulnerability, then writes a source patch that fixes it, on a private task set Vals runs every model through on its own harness. The column is the board's headline, which pools the PoC and patch tasks. Its task set differs from v1.1's, so the two are separate columns; v1 is kept for its field of 26 models, most never re-run on v1.1. Several models score 0% on the PoC half, which reads as refusal under Vals' harness rather than failure.
excludes: the PoC-only and patch-only task scores
CyberBench v1.1, which has a column of its own
CyberGym, an unrelated benchmark on similar OSS-Fuzz material

aa_omniscience_1_1.name: AA-Omniscience v1.1
aa_omniscience_1_1.description: Artificial Analysis' knowledge and hallucination benchmark: 3,000 questions (v1.1, since October 2026; down from v1's 6,000) over 42 economically relevant topics in six domains. The Omniscience Index is a bounded −100 to 100 score that rewards correct recall, penalises confident wrong answers and credits abstention; 0 means as often right as wrong.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1 values, on the 6,000-question set
the accuracy and hallucination-rate companions, which are columns of their own

aa_omniscience_1_0.name: AA-Omniscience v1
aa_omniscience_1_0.description: Artificial Analysis' knowledge and hallucination benchmark: 6,000 questions over 42 economically relevant topics in six domains. The Omniscience Index is a bounded −100 to 100 score that rewards correct recall, penalises confident wrong answers and credits abstention; 0 means as often right as wrong. Archived: v1, the 6,000-question set, as read until AA moved to v1.1 on 2026-10-27, kept for the models AA has not re-scored.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1.1 values, on the 3,000-question set
the accuracy and hallucination-rate companions, which are columns of their own

aa_omniscience_hallucination_1_1.name: AA-Omniscience v1.1 Hallucination Rate
aa_omniscience_hallucination_1_1.description: Companion metric to AA-Omniscience: of all responses that were not correct, the share that were confident wrong answers rather than partial answers or abstentions — incorrect / (incorrect + partial + not attempted). It measures what a model does when it does not know, so lower is better.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1 values, on the 6,000-question set
the non-hallucination rate, which is this metric inverted
the Omniscience Index and the accuracy companion

aa_omniscience_hallucination_1_0.name: AA-Omniscience v1 Hallucination Rate
aa_omniscience_hallucination_1_0.description: Companion metric to AA-Omniscience: of all responses that were not correct, the share that were confident wrong answers rather than partial answers or abstentions — incorrect / (incorrect + partial + not attempted). It measures what a model does when it does not know, so lower is better. Archived: v1, the 6,000-question set, as read until AA moved to v1.1 on 2026-10-27, kept for the models AA has not re-scored.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1.1 values, on the 3,000-question set
the non-hallucination rate, which is this metric inverted
the Omniscience Index and the accuracy companion

aa_omniscience_accuracy_1_1.name: AA-Omniscience v1.1 Accuracy
aa_omniscience_accuracy_1_1.description: Companion metric to AA-Omniscience: the plain share of the 3,000 questions (v1.1, since October 2026; down from v1's 6,000) answered correctly, before the Omniscience Index nets confident wrong answers off against it. Read next to the hallucination rate it is the other half of the same run — how much the model knows, against what it does with the rest.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1 values, on the 6,000-question set
the Omniscience Index and the hallucination-rate companion

aa_omniscience_accuracy_1_0.name: AA-Omniscience v1 Accuracy
aa_omniscience_accuracy_1_0.description: Companion metric to AA-Omniscience: the plain share of the 6,000 questions answered correctly, before the Omniscience Index nets confident wrong answers off against it. Read next to the hallucination rate it is the other half of the same run — how much the model knows, against what it does with the rest. Archived: v1, the 6,000-question set, as read until AA moved to v1.1 on 2026-10-27, kept for the models AA has not re-scored.
excludes: AA-Omniscience v1.1 values, on the 3,000-question set
the Omniscience Index and the hallucination-rate companion

simpleqa_verified.name: SimpleQA Verified
simpleqa_verified.description: Google DeepMind's cleaned 1,000-prompt successor to OpenAI's SimpleQA: short fact-seeking questions with one indisputable answer, after de-duplication, re-balancing of topics and correction of the original's wrong labels. Answers are graded correct, incorrect or not attempted, so a model that declines to guess loses less than one that confidently answers wrong. Run by Epoch AI on its own harness, the same for every model.
excludes: the original SimpleQA, a different and noisier question set

aa_lcr.name: AA-LCR
aa_lcr.description: Artificial Analysis Long Context Reasoning: 100 open-answer questions over real documents of 10k-100k tokens. Each needs multi-step reasoning that synthesises facts scattered across the text rather than a single lookup. Graded pass/fail by an LLM judge; metric is the average pass rate.
excludes: long-context tests that are not AA-LCR

critpt.name: CritPt
critpt.description: Complex Research using Integrated Thinking - Physics Test ("critical point"): 70 research-level physics challenges written by 50+ active researchers across 11 subfields, decomposed into 190 machine-verifiable checkpoint tasks. Deeply unsaturated: the best base models score in the low single digits.

critpt_2_0.name: CritPt v2
critpt_2_0.description: CritPt v2, the authors' revision of the research-level physics benchmark (underspecified statements, errors and typos corrected), on the full set of 70 composite research challenges. Models work with a code-execution tool in an offline Linux sandbox; answers (Python functions, symbolic expressions, numbers) go to the official grading server, scored as pass@1 challenge accuracy. Artificial Analysis runs it and publishes the score on its evaluation page only, for the models charted there; critpt.com's leaderboard shows the same numbers. Not comparable with v1, which is the full set with no tools, nor with the 40-challenge hard subset.

critpt_hard_2_0.name: CritPt v2 Hard
critpt_hard_2_0.description: CritPt v2, the authors' revision of the research-level physics benchmark (underspecified statements, errors and typos corrected), on its hard subset: 40 of the 70 composite research challenges. Models work with a code-execution tool in an offline Linux sandbox; answers (Python functions, symbolic expressions, numbers) go to the official grading server, scored as pass@1 challenge accuracy over five repeats. Artificial Analysis runs it as a component of its Intelligence Index v5.0. Not comparable with v1, which is the full set with no tools, nor with v2's full 70-challenge set.

aime_2026.name: AIME 2026
aime_2026.description: American Invitational Mathematics Examination, 2026: both papers, 30 questions in total, each a 3-hour exam with integer answers from 0 to 999. Published runs average repeated single attempts rather than taking the best of several, so a mean over k samples is the same measurement as pass@1 and a best-of-k is not.

aime_2025.name: AIME 2025
aime_2025.description: American Invitational Mathematics Examination, 2025: both papers, 30 questions in total, each a 3-hour exam with integer answers from 0 to 999. Published runs average repeated single attempts rather than taking the best of several, so a mean over k samples is the same measurement as pass@1 and a best-of-k is not.

hmmt_feb_2026.name: HMMT February 2026
hmmt_feb_2026.description: The 30 problems of the February 2026 Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, each with a single final answer. Set after most models' training cutoff, so it is uncontaminated in the way AIME 2025 no longer is. MathArena runs it independently; most values here are lab self-reports of the same problems.

frontiermath_tier_4.name: FrontierMath Tier 4
frontiermath_tier_4.description: The research-level tier of Epoch AI's FrontierMath: problems written by research mathematicians to take a specialist days, each with an automatically checkable answer. The v2 private set, run by Epoch on its own harness with a Python tool for computation, the same for every model. The hardest mathematics column in the table, with the widest spread at the top.
excludes: self-reported FrontierMath numbers naming no tier

frontiermath_tiers_1_3.name: FrontierMath Tiers 1-3
frontiermath_tiers_1_3.description: Epoch AI's unpublished, expert-written mathematics problems from undergraduate-hard to research level, each with an automatically checkable answer. The v2 private set, run by Epoch on its own harness with a Python tool for computation, the same for every model; problems are never released, so the column cannot be trained on.
excludes: self-reported FrontierMath numbers naming no tier

gpqa_diamond.name: GPQA Diamond
gpqa_diamond.description: Graduate-level Google-proof multiple-choice science questions (biology, physics, chemistry) from GPQA; Diamond split used in evals.
excludes: GPQA main and extended, different question sets

hle_diamond.name: Humanity's Last Exam Diamond
hle_diamond.description: HLE-Diamond, the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI's refined subset of Humanity's Last Exam: 1,000 questions, 500 testing reasoning and 500 testing expert knowledge, kept after a year of cleaning with input from the research community so that each has a verified answer and can be answered closed-book. A different question set from the 2,500-question HLE, so its own column rather than a reading of that one. Every value is the maintainers' own run, published with the release: each model at the highest reasoning effort it offers (max for GPT, Claude and Muse, xhigh for Grok, high for Gemini, Kimi and GLM), without tools. GLM 5.3, which takes no images, was run on the text-only questions only.
excludes: with-tools runs (web search and code execution), worth +19 to +31 points on the models the maintainers ran both ways
the maintainers' reasoning-high view, every model held at high, up to 6 points lower
the full 2,500-question HLE and HLE-Verified, different question sets
the reasoning-only or knowledge-only half on its own

hle.name: Humanity's Last Exam
hle.description: Humanity's Last Exam, run without tools: 2,500 expert-level questions across mathematics, the humanities and the natural sciences, written to resist internet retrieval. This column is the no-tools variant only. Tool use changes the answer rather than sharpening it -- across the models whose publisher states both, search and a code interpreter are worth a median +11.5 points and up to +27 -- so with-tools and search-agent runs are rejected rather than blended in here. Most values are Artificial Analysis' own run of the 2,158-question text-only subset, pass@1, and track AA's current implementation of it.
excludes: with-tools and search-agent runs, worth a median +11.5 points and up to +27

arc_agi_3.name: ARC-AGI-3
arc_agi_3.description: ARC Prize's third abstraction-and-reasoning benchmark and the first interactive one: instead of completing a grid from examples, the agent is dropped into novel game-like environments and has to explore, infer the goal and the rules, and act on them. Scored on the semi-private set ARC Prize runs itself, in its own harness, taking each model's best published effort. Far from saturated where ARC-AGI-2 is close to it.
excludes: Provider Adapter runs, in the provider's own agent harness

arc_agi_2.name: ARC-AGI-2
arc_agi_2.description: ARC Prize's second abstraction-and-reasoning corpus: novel grid-transformation puzzles that a person solves from two or three examples, built so that memorised knowledge does not help. Scored on the semi-private evaluation set ARC Prize verifies itself. The head of the field is close to the ceiling; its interactive successor, ARC-AGI-3, is the unsaturated one. Read from ARC Prize's own board, with Epoch AI's copy of it filling the rest.
excludes: Provider Adapter runs, in the provider's own agent harness

arc_agi_1.name: ARC-AGI-1
arc_agi_1.description: The original abstraction-and-reasoning corpus: grid-transformation puzzles solved from a few examples. Scored on the semi-private set ARC Prize verifies itself, best published effort per model. Long saturated at the top and superseded by ARC-AGI-2 and -3; kept as a column for the older and smaller models it still separates.

mmlu_pro.name: MMLU-Pro
mmlu_pro.description: TIGER-Lab's reasoning-focused rebuild of MMLU: around 12,000 questions across 14 disciplines with ten answer options instead of four, after the trivial and mislabelled items MMLU had accumulated were filtered out. The extra distractors and the chain-of-thought scoring shift it from recall toward reasoning. Metric is accuracy.
excludes: MMLU-ProX and KMMLU-Pro, a multilingual extension and a Korean one

mmmlu.name: MMMLU
mmmlu.description: OpenAI's multilingual MMLU: the MMLU test set professionally translated by human translators into 14 languages (Arabic, Bengali, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Brazilian Portuguese, Swahili, Yoruba and Simplified Chinese), scored as the average accuracy over them. The table's only measurement of non-English knowledge. Lab self-reports; the head of the field is compressed.
excludes: machine-translated sets such as Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX

mmmu_pro.name: MMMU Pro
mmmu_pro.description: Vision-centric extension of MMMU that rigorously evaluates large multimodal models on challenging, college-level tasks requiring expert, cross‑disciplinary understanding and integrated visual–text reasoning.
excludes: MMMU, which is not the Pro set
the 4-option set (Vals AI's "MMMU Pro" board), which reads several points higher

zerobench.name: ZeroBench
zerobench.description: Deliberately "impossible" visual reasoning benchmark: 100 hand-crafted, multi-step questions over natural and synthetic images, scored as accuracy on the main set. Built for headroom — open-weight models sit in the low tens of percent, and the 334 subquestions are a separate score series this column does not mix in.
excludes: the 334 subquestions, which score three to four times higher

osworld_2_1.name: OSWorld 2.1
osworld_2_1.description: Long-horizon computer use: 108 end-to-end workflows across seven professional domains — research, creative production, engineering, business and finance, administration, healthcare, personal services — run in a desktop VM against 31 self-hosted websites and stateful user data, each taking a skilled human a median of about 1.6 hours. Tasks hinge on cross-source reasoning, hidden state the instruction never states, messages that change the task mid-run and questions the agent has to put to a simulated user. Scored by binary accuracy — the share of tasks fully completed, the authors' primary metric — on the full set at a 500-step budget, taking the best of a model's published reasoning-effort and tool settings. This column is release 2.1, the bug-fix release the maintainers now recommend, as run on the benchmark's own board. It re-pins task files, assets and mocked websites, and scores do not carry across releases — Claude Opus 5 at max effort reads 44.3 here and 31.4 on 2026.08.08 — so each release is its own column. No tracked model is scored on it yet. Scores labs report themselves are filed under OSWorld 2.0 Vendor.

osworld_2_0_2026_06_24.name: OSWorld 2.0 2026.06.24
osworld_2_0_2026_06_24.description: Long-horizon computer use: 108 end-to-end workflows across seven professional domains — research, creative production, engineering, business and finance, administration, healthcare, personal services — run in a desktop VM against 31 self-hosted websites and stateful user data, each taking a skilled human a median of about 1.6 hours. Tasks hinge on cross-source reasoning, hidden state the instruction never states, messages that change the task mid-run and questions the agent has to put to a simulated user. Scored by binary accuracy — the share of tasks fully completed, the authors' primary metric — on the full set at a 500-step budget, taking the best of a model's published reasoning-effort and tool settings. This column is release 2026.06.24, the one the paper reports, as run on the benchmark's own board. The task set has been re-released since (2026.08.08, then the bug-fix 2.1) with new task files, assets and mocked websites, and scores do not carry across releases — Claude Opus 5 at max effort reads 31.4 on 2026.08.08 and 44.3 on 2.1 — so 2026.08.08 has a column of its own and 2.1 gets one once enough models are scored on it. Scores labs report themselves are filed under OSWorld 2.0 Vendor.

osworld_2_0_2026_08_08.name: OSWorld 2.0 2026.08.08
osworld_2_0_2026_08_08.description: Long-horizon computer use: 108 end-to-end workflows across seven professional domains — research, creative production, engineering, business and finance, administration, healthcare, personal services — run in a desktop VM against 31 self-hosted websites and stateful user data, each taking a skilled human a median of about 1.6 hours. Tasks hinge on cross-source reasoning, hidden state the instruction never states, messages that change the task mid-run and questions the agent has to put to a simulated user. Scored by binary accuracy — the share of tasks fully completed, the authors' primary metric — on the full set at a 500-step budget, taking the best of a model's published reasoning-effort and tool settings. This column is release 2026.08.08, the first re-release, as run on the benchmark's own board. It re-pins task files, assets and mocked websites, and scores do not carry across releases — Claude Opus 5 at max effort reads 31.4 here and 44.3 on the bug-fix 2.1 — so 2026.06.24 and 2.1 are separate columns. Scores labs report themselves are filed under OSWorld 2.0 Vendor.

osworld_2_0_vendor.name: OSWorld 2.0 Vendor
osworld_2_0_vendor.description: OSWorld 2.0 as each model's own lab reports it — the model card or launch post, as republished by llm-stats — rather than a run from the benchmark's own board. Labs do not agree on what they report: some give binary accuracy (the share of tasks fully completed), others the partial checkpoint score, which reads two to three times higher; some ran release 2026.06.24, others 2026.08.08 or 2.1, on the full 108-task set or the 82-task offline set, and many do not say which. The column follows llm-stats and files every headline as published, so it compares a lab's models with each other, not one lab with another; the official release columns beside it are the controlled comparison.

osworld_verified.name: OSWorld-Verified
osworld_verified.description: Benchmark measuring GUI agents' ability to complete real computer tasks in a sandboxed Ubuntu environment, scored by task success rate. The benchmark's own board is read first, on its Foundation E2E GUI setup at max 100 steps; a model it has not run carries the OSWorld-Verified score its lab reports (model card, launch post, or an aggregator republishing one), whose step budget and harness are the lab's own.

mathvista_mini.name: MathVista-mini
mathvista_mini.description: Mathematical reasoning in visual contexts — figure QA, geometry, math word problems, textbook and visual QA — scored as answer accuracy on MathVista's 1,000-example testmini split, the split published runs report.

charxiv_reasoning.name: CharXiv Reasoning
charxiv_reasoning.description: Reasoning over scientific charts: 2,323 figures taken from arXiv papers, each with four open-ended reasoning questions whose answers have to be read off the chart itself rather than recalled. This column is the reasoning split ("RQ") without tool use — the descriptive split is a different, far easier question set, and a run allowed a code interpreter is a different measurement again.
excludes: the descriptive split, a far easier question set
runs allowed a code interpreter, worth about 6 points
